abstract: Summary Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL) is an aggressive lymphoma associated with Epstein–Barr virus which does not respond to conventional anthracycline-based chemotherapy. Recent multi-omics studies have identified genetic and epigenetic alterations involved in the tumor pathogenesis and enabled the characterisation of distinct molecular subtypes with therapeutic and prognostic implications. Similarly, genomic and transcriptomic studies have shed new light on the tumor microenvironment (TME) and potential interactions with the EBV-infected malignant cells, as well as their potential influence on tumor development and progression. This review provides an update on the key genetic alterations and analysis of the recurrent mutations of ENKTL, the role of EBV, epigenetic modifications and emerging molecular classifications of both the tumor and the TME. We also explore the prognostic and therapeutic applications of these new insights, and how they are beginning to reshape the current understanding and future clinical management of this difficult-to-treat disease.

Introduction
Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL) is an aggressive lymphoma associated with Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) infection. It can arise from NK or cytotoxic T cells and the disease shows a distinct predilection for East Asian and indigenous South/Central American populations, accounting for 28.6%–31% of T/NK lymphomas in Asia, but only 8% in Europe and North America.
1
,
2
Majority (about 80%) of ENKTL patients present with nasal disease involving the upper aerodigestive tract. Some tumors manifest in non-nasal sites such as the skin, gastrointestinal tract and testis. There is a strong association with EBV, which occurs in the tumour cells in a clonal episomal form and exhibits a type II latency pattern characterized by positive expression of LMP1, LMP2A and EBNA1.
3
Despite the universal association with EBV, the exact role of the virus in this lymphoma is not well understood. When diagnosed at an early stage (Stage I/II), patients treated with intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) combined with optimal chemotherapy yielded 5-year progression-free survivals (PFS) of >60% and overall survival (OS) >70%.
4
Prognosis is poorer in advanced stage disease, with the Phase II study of the now widely-used
l
-asparaginase-based SMILE regimen reporting a 5-year disease-free survival (DFS) of 64% and OS of 50%.
5
Another study reported disease progression within 5 years in over 70% of patients with advanced stage disease.
6
In the relapsed/refractory setting, survival is particularly dismal, with a reported median PFS of 4.1 months and OS of 6.4 months.
7
The prognostic index of natural killer lymphoma–EBV (PINK-E) index, is useful to predict outcome based on non–anthracycline-containing regimens or radiotherapy with curative intent
8
and age >60 years, stage III/IV disease, distant nodal involvement, non-nasal clinical subtype disease, and quantifiable plasma EBV predict an unfavorable clinical outcome.
In recent years, significant strides have been made in unraveling the molecular mechanisms driving ENKTL pathogenesis. Advancements in multi-omics studies have identified distinct molecular subtypes of the tumor with prognostic and therapeutic implications. A recent study identified 3 molecular subtypes of ENKTL based on genomic and transcriptomic signatures—tumor suppressor-immune modular (TSIM), MGA-BRDT (MB), and HDAC9-EP300-ARID1A (HEA) subtypes, which are associated with different prognosis.
9
Since then, several groups have also proposed other classification methods that were found to correlate with clinicopathological features and disease prognosis.
10
,
11

12
In addition, emerging data also highlights how components of the tumor microenvironment (TME) actively shape tumor biology, mediate immune evasion, and modulate responses to treatments.
This review summarizes these emerging concepts and advancements in the understanding of the molecular landscape of the tumor, and the role of the microenvironment in ENKTL. Key genetic alterations, epigenetic modifications, EBV viral oncogenesis and emerging molecular classifications will be discussed together with the therapeutic and prognostic implications of these findings, which provide insights towards personalized treatment approaches to improve patient outcomes.
Search strategies and selection criteria
References for this Review were identified through searches of PubMed with the search terms “NK/T lymphoma” and its permutations, “tumor microenvironment”, “genomic”, “transcriptomic” and “epigenetic” from 2018 to present. Articles were also identified through searches of the authors’ own files. Only papers published in English were reviewed. The final reference list was generated on the basis of originality and relevance to the broad scope of this Review.

miRNA/non-coding RNAs
Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) account for up to 98% of all human RNAs. These include microRNAs (miRNAs), small nuclear RNAs, PIWI-interacting RNAs, long non-coding RNAs (lncRNA), and circular RNAs. These RNAs, while not translated into proteins, are implicated in diverse cellular functions and their role in cancer and other diseases is being elucidated.
59
In ENKTL, the role of aberrantly expressed ncRNAs is only starting to be understood. Among these are miRNAs, short single stranded ncRNAs encoded by the host or EBV. Dysregulation of human miRNAs may play pathogenetic roles, including the activation of AKT signaling via overexpression of miR-21 and miR-155,
60
and downregulation of NFkB activity by miR-146a, which functions as a TSG.
61
Additionally, targets of downregulated miRNAs are enriched for genes involved in cell cycle-related, p53, and MAPK signaling pathways.
62
Other overexpressed miRNAs include miR-494-3p, miR-142-3p, miR-155 and downregulated miRNAs include miR-150, miR-15a, miR-16 and miR-205.
63
Long non-coding RNAs (LncRNAs), usually >200 nucleotides in length, are thought to regulate gene expression by transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms. Whole transcriptome sequencing analysis has identified 232 lncRNAs that are dysregulated in ENKTL, including SNHG5, ZFAS1, and MIR155HG suggesting their potential role in lymphomagenesis.
64
Molecular classification of ENKTL
In recent years, the genetic subtyping of ENKTL has garnered considerable attention, revealing distinct genomic subtypes with significant implications for prognosis and treatment strategies (
Table 2
). The first significant attempt at such subtyping was conducted by Xiong and colleagues in 2020.
9
They performed a comprehensive multi-omics study that combined whole genome sequencing (WGS), whole exome sequencing (WES), array-based copy-number variation (CNV) analysis, and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) on a large cohort of 100 well-characterized ENKTL patient samples. Based on RNA-seq data and genomic alterations, they proposed three ENKTL genetic subtypes: tumor suppressor-immune modular (TSIM), MGA-BRDT (MB), and HDAC9-EP300-ARID1A (HEA). These subtypes correlate with the cell of origin, EBV pattern, and specific genomic alterations.

activation, has an excellent prognosis, with a 3-year OS rate of 91.7%.
Subsequent sub-clustering of malignant cells using pseudotime mapping by the same authors uncovered 3 clusters of malignant cells, which correlated with the 3 molecular subtypes. The TSIM subtype is associated with the NK cluster (Cluster 3) with increased EBV gene expression, induction of cell cycle progression and genomic instability. The MB subtype corresponded to the T/NK progenitor cluster (cluster 1) and characterized by activation of hematopoietic progenitor genes and metastasis prone phenotype while the HEA subtype is associated with the T-cluster (cluster 2) which showed activation of genes enriched in TCR signaling pathway and T helper cell differentiation.
65
Building on this, Dong et al.
10

Each subgroup exhibits unique genetic characteristics and differing prognostic outcomes. Cluster C1 shows high copy number complexity, with gains in 17q21 (
STAT3

MYC

JAK3

TP53, BCOR

More recently, a genome-wide analysis comparing primary and relapsed/refractory ENKTL patients (163 total; 127 primary, 36 relapsed/refractory) revealed distinct mutational profiles and elevated levels of genomic instability in relapsed/refractory cases.
11
This includes events such as single nucleotide variations (SNVs), copy number variants (CNVs), insertions/deletions (INDELs), and structural variants such as chromothripsis, focal amplifications, and extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNAs). A five-cluster (C0–C4) molecular subtyping system was devised by integrating recurrent genomic alterations at both nucleotide and structural levels, providing further prognostic information and treatment guidance, particularly for patients with relapsed/refractory disease.
Lastly, Ito and colleagues
12

CDKN

A
and
TP

KDM

A
and

EBV and tumorigenesis
EBV is a ubiquitous oncogenic herpesvirus that afflicts up to 90% of the population worldwide.
66
Its presence in clonal and episomal forms within tumor cells supports its oncogenic role in ENKTL. Most patients with ENKTL are infected by EBV subtype A and express latency II program. A notable variant of EBV containing a 30-bp deletion in the latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1) gene, is associated with poor prognosis and is more frequently observed in Asian ENKTL patients compared to those in Latin America. These regional differences in EBV strains and LMP1 variants likely reflect geographic variations in strain types rather than distinctions in disease pathogenesis or host immune response.
27
,
67
,
68
In ENKTL, EBV exhibits a type II latency pattern characterized by the presence of EBV nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1) and LMP1 and the absence of EBNA2.
69
LMP1 expression was found to be a predictor of poorer prognosis in ENKTL.
70
,
71
LMP1 is a viral protein expressed in most EBV-associated lymphoproliferative diseases. It consists of a short cytoplasmic amino-terminus, six transmembrane domains (amino acids 25–186), and a cytoplasmic carboxy-terminal signaling domain which contains the transformation effector sites, TES 1 and 2. These sites are responsible for the interaction of LMP1 with cellular signaling molecules of the TRAF family and TRADD and the activation of NF-κB and JNK/AP1 signaling.
72
In ENKTL, which is virtually always associated with EBV infection, LMP-1 is thought to be one of the major drivers of lymphomagenesis. It is believed to cause malignant transformation via activation of the NF-κB,
73
mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK),
74
phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3-K),
75
IRF7,
76
MYC
20
and STAT pathways
77
dysregulation of cytokine and chemokine production, immune modulation, alteration of microRNA expression patterns, as well as cell interaction and migration.
72
,
78
Aside from its oncogenic role, LMP1 also reshapes the cellular landscape and promotes an immunosuppressive microenvironment in ENKTL (see section 2.2).
79
Therefore, targeting LMP1+ tumor cells may be a potential therapeutic strategy in ENKTL.
Phylogenetic analyses of independent Chinese cohorts have demonstrated that EBV sequences from ENKTL showed close similarity to those found in nasopharyngeal carcinoma, with EBV- isolates clustering according to geographic origin. This provides compelling genetic evidence for the geographic prevalence of ENKTL in Asian populations.
9
,
67
,
80
Nevertheless, EBV-isolates derived from one disease tend to cluster together and separately from other cancers, suggesting disease-specific EBV sequences.
67
In addition, although the complete EBV particle is epigenetic-naive, it is believed that the virus hijacks the host's DNMTs to affect methylation modifications on the infected cells to evade host immune surveillance. The pattern of methylation appears to differ between EBV-associated malignancies. Significant differences of EBV CpG sites, particularly those located on gene BILF2, were observed between ENKTL and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
67
,
81
A recent single cell multi-omics study integrating genomic and transcriptomic data with mass spectrometry-based proteomics analysis found EBV peptides spanning the whole viral genome in ENKTL tumor samples. Using the genes identified, the authors proceeded with
in vitro

in vivo

65
EBV is also believed to drive oncogenesis via the regulation of 44 EBV miRNAs.
82
Some of these key mechanisms include inhibition of
TP53

Frequent intragenic deletions of the EBV genome have been reported, especially affecting BART microRNA clusters and may reactivate the lytic cycle through the upregulation of
BZLF1
and

EBV and the microenvironment
In addition to its role in lymphomagenesis, EBV has also been found to alter the immune microenvironment in ENKTL. A recent study by Li et al. identified six distinct malignant NK cell clusters, each characterized by unique transcriptomic signatures and differential expression of EBV-encoded genes.
79
Among these, one specific malignant NK cluster with unique expression of
LMP1
showed upregulation of JAK/STAT and NF-kB oncogenic signaling pathways. This cluster also expresses immune checkpoint molecules, CD86 and PD-L1, and exhibits intense immunosuppressive interactions with T cells through CD86-CTLA4 and PDL1-PD1, suggesting that LMP1 may be a crucial driver triggering tumorigenesis and promoting tumor growth.
Interestingly, despite inducing a stronger immunosuppressive TME, ENKTL patients with high expression of EBV-encoded genes are associated with high HLA-II expression and better survival outcomes compared to patients with low expression of EBV-encoded genes, possibly related to profound immune activation, enhanced antigen presentation and stronger immune response of CD4+ T cells and cytotoxic cells which eventually result in a strengthened anti-tumor immunity.
79
Three major clusters of lymphoma microenvironment (LME) phenotypes with distinct immune cell compositions have recently been identified using single-cell transcriptomes.
65
LME1 cluster is associated with immune-desert phenotype and entirely devoid of T and MDC cell infiltration. LME2 shows an immune-deficient phenotype with disabled innate immunity featuring presence of T and stromal cells but absence of MDC cells and LME3, the immune-inflamed phenotype, is characterized by high levels of both T and MDC cell infiltration, and association with immune activation and exhaustion. The three LME clusters demonstrated dysregulation of G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) signaling which is regulated by EBV and involved in cancer immunity cycle progression. Notably, high expression of chemokine receptor-1 (CCR1) was identified in LME1 and LME3. Overexpression of CCR1 on malignant and immunosuppressive cells modulated virus–cancer interaction on microenvironment. Notably, therapeutic targeting CCR1 resulted in T-cell activation, EBV eradication, and killing of tumor cells in ENKTL organoid.
65
Tumor microenvironment/immune checkpoint inhibition
The TME is a complex ecosystem comprising immune cells, stromal cells, extracellular matrix and cytokines that plays a critical role in cancer biology by creating an immunosuppressive environment allowing tumor growth.
86
A recent genomic and transcriptomic profiling study has identified four microenvironment-based subtypes in peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL) with discrete patterns of gene expression, different immune communities, and distinct potential vulnerabilities to targeted agents.
87
Similarly, in ENKTL, there is a growing corpus of work demonstrating how the immune milieu is altered in disease.
Malignant NK cells can actively regulate the recruitment of immune cells to the TME. Li et al. demonstrated TME heterogeneity in ENKTL using single cell RNA sequencing and reported that malignant NK cells express high levels of chemokines, such as CCL3, CCL4 and CCL5, which interact with immune cells to recruit them into the TME. Tumor cells also secrete dipeptidylpeptidase IV (
DPP4
), which may inhibit the recruitment of normal NK cells by degrading chemokines such as CXCLs.
79
Malignant NK cells, especially those expressing LMP1, and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) jointly promote an immunosuppressive TME in ENKTL. TAMs were found to express specific chemokines, such as CCL2/CCL3/CCL8, that have the potential to interact with CCR1 and CCR2 on monocytes, CXCL2/CXCL9/CXCL10, that can interact with CXCR2 and CXCR3 on normal NK cells, and CXCL9/CXCL10, that recognises CXCR3 on T cells, suggesting that TAMs may play a role in recruitment of both monocytes and cytotoxic immune cells from peripheral blood to the tumor. Furthermore, single cell analyses demonstrated that TAMs crosstalk with tumor infiltrating T cells via CD80/CD86-CTLA4, PDL1/PDL2-PD1, and LGALS9-HAVCR2 interactions, which result in an immunosuppressive effect on exhausted and regulatory T cells. These data were supported by multiplex immunofluorescent staining assays that showed physical juxtaposition of PDL1-expressing TAMs with CD8+ T cells within the tumors.
79
In line with the data, a high proportion of TAMs and higher expression of TAM marker, CD206 protein, in tumors are associated with worse overall survival.
79
The impaired anti-tumor immune response in ENKTL may be due to the upregulation of inhibitory receptors, such as CTLA4, PD1, TIM3, and TIGIT, resulting in impaired effector cytokine secretion and T cell dysfunction. The PD-1/PD-L1 pathway negatively regulates immune response by preventing the activation and proliferation of effector T cells, reducing interferon γ (IFNγ) production, thus contributing to T-cell exhaustion and an immunosuppressive environment.
88
Therefore, restoring T cell function using immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) represents a promising strategy in ENKTL treatment. The upregulation of PD-L1 in ENKTL may be a consequence of LMP1-driven activation of MAPK/NF-κB signaling or phosphorylation and activation of STAT3 due to mutation of STAT3.
89
,
90
Wai et al. further showed the upregulation of PD-L1 in EBV-associated T/NK cell lymphomas, including ENKTL, may be related to activation of IFNγ, IL6_JAK_STAT3 and NFκB pathways.
49
Studies have reported the overexpression of PD-L1 in tumor cells of ENKTL but most of them employed conventional singleplex immunohistochemistry and it can be difficult to distinguish PD-L1 expression in tumor from immune cells, including macrophages. Zhang et al. performed PD-L1/CD14 double stain and demonstrated that higher percentage (≥24.2%) of PD-L1+ monocytes in tumor tissues exhibited a significantly inferior survival.
91
Additionally, the percentage of PD-L1+ monocytes in the blood of ENKTL patients was higher than that in healthy individuals and positively correlated with that in tumor tissues. Similar to tumor tissues, a higher percentage of PD-L1+ monocytes in blood was an independent adverse prognostic factor.
91
Another study utilizing EBER/PD-L1 double stain demonstrated that PD-L1 positivity in tumor and immune cells was associated with low international prognostic index but not with overall survival.
91
,
92
A recent study identified high coexpression of PD-L1 and IDO1 in tumor cells to be associated with poor overall survival (OS) in a large cohort of ENKTL patients. Interestingly, the high-risk group in their nomogram model constructed with PD-L1 and IDO1 expression was associated with high CD4+ T cell infiltration and high expression of multiple immunosuppressive molecules, such as CD276, TIGIT, CTLA4 and IL2RA. The poor OS may be related to the immunosuppressive effects of Treg cells and PD-L1 and IDO1 might be potential targets for future immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy.
93
The TME can evolve with disease progression and may serve as a useful biomarker for immunotherapy. Based on the expression of 579 immune-related genes, four tumor immune microenvironment subgroups of ENKTL were identified. The immune tolerance (IT) group was characterized by high-Treg counts and associated with the best OS. The immune-silenced (IS) group is associated with immune exhaustion and low expression of immune-related genes, advanced stage and worse OS. The immune evasion (IE) group displayed high cytotoxic T-cell counts, high PD-L1 expression, low Treg counts and an intermediate OS. One patient in the IT group responded to pembrolizumab, an anti-PD-1 antibody, and none of 5 patients responded in the IS group. Two patients showed a shift of subgroups from IT to IE with disease progression.
94
The authors also demonstrated that pre-treatment FDG PET/CT findings can predict TME subtypes. Findings such as high SUVmax, high metabolic tumor volume, high total lesion glycolysis and presence of adrenal or testicular lesion favored the IS subtype, which is associated with worse OS compared to non-IS subtypes.
95
Until recently, most of the work on the role of epigenetic changes in cancer has focused on the neoplastic cells. Given the relevance of the immune cells and microenvironment in cancer, there has been growing interest in the epigenetic alterations that affect immune cell function in the TME.
96
It has been shown in several cancer types that loss-of-function mutations in KMT2 family epigenetic modifiers are associated with better treatment response to immune checkpoint inhibitors,
97
suggesting that epigenetic aberrations in neoplastic cells likely exert an influence on the tumour immune microenvironment. Given that some of the most highly mutated genes in ENKTL, such as
KMT2D, TET2, BCOR
and
EP300
, are epigenetic modifiers,
24
,
25
,
29
,
50
,
53
more work needs to be done to study the impact of these mutations on the TME and the consequent therapeutic implication, in terms of response to immune checkpoint inhibitors.
Clinical implications
Therapeutic implications
Traditional anticancer therapies have primarily focused on targeting the malignant cell population. However, an emerging understanding of the complex role of the TME in tumor biology and cross-talks between tumor and the TME presents novel therapeutic strategies targeting both tumor and TME to disrupt this mutual support system. Integrating this knowledge into treatment regimens opens avenues for more effective cancer management, including combination therapies that modulate the TME to enhance immune responses and overcome treatment resistance.
79
,
94
Tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs) have been shown to play an active role in creating an immunosuppressive environment via their unique cytokine profile and crosstalk with other immune cells in ENKTL
79
and strategies to deplete, reprogram or block TAM-mediated immunosuppression are being evaluated, including disruption of the colony-stimulating factor-1 (CSF-1)/CSF-1 receptor (CSF-1R) signaling pathway that is essential for the recruitment and functional regulation of TAMs,
98
,
99
and blocking CCL2-CCR2 signaling to prevent their mobilisation from the bone marrow.
100
The recognition of distinct TME signatures in ENKTL may also influence precision immunotherapy. The response rate to pembrolizumab, an anti-PD-1 antibody, has been shown to correspond to the TME phenotype, with 100% response rate in the immune tolerance group, 60% in the immune evasion group, and 0% in the immune-silenced group, thus suggesting that the TME phenotype may potentially be helpful in stratifying patients based on predicted response to immunotherapy.
94
Xiong and co-workers similarly classified the ENKTL lymphoma microenvironment into 3 categories and they identified high expression of chemokine receptor CCR1 in malignant cells in the immunedesert group which is devoid of T cells and myeloid dendritic cells.
65
The authors postulated that CCR1 expression results in T cell exhaustion and CCR1 blockade with the compound, CCX354-C, was effective in expansion of cytotoxic cell subsets and tumour killing.
65

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) and
c
hallenges limiting the efficacy of ICI therapy
Under normal physiological conditions, immune checkpoints maintain immune homeostasis by balancing inhibitory and stimulatory pathways that regulate immune cell activity. Many cancers exploit these mechanisms to suppress immune activity, allowing tumor cells to evade immune detection. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) work by blocking inhibitory checkpoint pathways, thereby restoring T-cell activity and promoting sustained immune responses against cancer.
Programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) and programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) are some of the most extensively studied inhibitory checkpoint molecules. Current trials (
NCT04417166
,
NCT03728972
) are examining pembrolizumab in previously untreated early-stage ENKTL, while studies of various PD-1 inhibitors (e.g. pembrolizumab, nivolumab and sintilimab) are ongoing in the relapsed/refractory setting.
102
,
103
,
104
Although PD-1 inhibitors have shown efficacy in relapsed/refractory T-cell lymphomas,
105
they have yet to become standard of care in ENKTL, in both the upfront and relapsed/refractory settings. Challenges limiting the efficacy of ICI therapy in lymphoma may be related to the following i) defective antigen presentation, ii) non-inflamed TME and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), iii) immunosuppressive metabolites, iv) lack of predictive biomarkers of response, v) genetic factors
106
and vi) adverse effects of ICI.
Defective antigen presentation (AP) can arise due to loss or deregulation of MHC-I and MHC-II driven AP machinery or dysregulation of enzymes needed for AP, including gamma-interferon-inducible-lysosomal thiol reductase (GILT) and human leukocyte antigen DM (HLA-DM). Combination therapy with MHC-independent treatments, such as chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy (CAR T-cell therapy) or bispecific T-cell engager antibodies (BiTEs) are alternatives to overcome the defective AP.
Many lymphomas harbor a ‘non-inflamed’ TME characterized by low infiltration of immune cells and plethora of genetic alterations to enable immune evasion and pose challenge to ICI therapy. In ENKTL, Cho and coworkers demonstrated that in the immune-silenced (IS) group associated with advanced stage disease, there is also immune exhaustion and low expression of immune-related genes.
94
Similarly, an immune-desert phenotype entirely devoid of T and MDC cell infiltration has also been identified by Xiong et al.
65
Upregulation of other inhibitory checkpoint molecules, besides PD1-PDL1, may also contribute to ICI therapy resistance, including lymphocyte activation gene-3 (LAG-3) and T cell immunoglobulin and mucin-domain-containing-3 (TIM-3). He and colleagues recently reported that another immune checkpoint of the B7 family, V-domain immunoglobulin suppressor of T-cell activation (VISTA), is aberrantly expressed in ENKTL and high expression of both PD-L1 and VISTA had the worst outcomes and resistance to PD-1 blockade.
107
TAMs play a key role in tumor biology by promoting immunosuppression and phagocytosis. Li et al. recently demonstrated that TAMs together with tumor cells, jointly promote an immunosuppressive TME in ENKTL by exerting immunosuppressive interactions with exhausted and regulatory T cells. Additionally, a high level of TAMs within the tumor was correlated with worse overall survival.
79
It has been postulated that combining PD-1 blockade with macrophage depleting therapies such as anti-CSF antibodies or the promotion of inflammatory macrophages through phosphatidyl 3-kinase-γ inhibitors may have a synergistic effect.
108
Immunosuppressive metabolites, such as indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1) can contribute to ICI resistance. IDO1 converts tryptophan to kynurenine in the TME which causes T-cell anergy, apoptosis and suppression of T effector cell function. A recent study identified high coexpression of PD-L1 and IDO1 in tumor cells to be associated with poor overall survival (OS).
93
IDO1 inhibitor epacadostat (
NCT03322384
) is currently being investigated in lymphoma as a synergistic cancer therapeutic agent with ICIs that could overcome immunosuppressive metabolites.
Although reports have demonstrated the efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 blockade in relapsed/refractory ENKTL,
109
,
110
the relationship between PD-L1 expression and the efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 blockade remains inconsistent. This may be due to different cut-offs used for defining positive or high expression, different clones of antibodies and the challenge in distinguishing expression in tumors from immune cells based on conventional singleplex immunohistochemistry. It has been recently demonstrated that therapeutic response to pembrolizumab may be better predicted by the presence of structural rearrangements disrupting the 3′-UTR region of PD-L1, than just the absolute level of PD-L1 expression.
111
Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop better biomarkers that can predict response to ICI therapy in lymphomas.
Different genetic and epigenetic factors in the TME and tumor compartment may render ICIs ineffective. These include alterations in the oncogenes and TSG implicated in the pathogenesis of ENKTL, such as EZH2, MYC and TP53, which can contribute towards immune cell exhaustion and suppression. For example, EZH2-mediated histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) has been reported to suppress the production of T helper 1 (TH1)-type chemokines CXCL9 and CXCL10, and as a result, reduce the recruitment of effector T-cells to the TME.
112
Overactivation of MYC may initiate tumor-induced immune suppression via crosstalk with various immune cell subsets in the TME, such as T cells, B cells, TAMs and natural killer cells, as well as by inhibiting effector T cells.
113
TP53
is the most frequently mutated gene in ENKTL and mutations in
TP53
can also affect T-cell recruitment and activity, leading to immune evasion and promoting cancer progression.
114
While anti-PD1 therapy has demonstrated efficacy in some ENKTL patients, its effectiveness remains inconsistent and unpredictable and may even result in adverse outcomes. In addition, in patients in whom ICIs manage to trigger an anti-tumor immune response, there is also a need to ensure that this balance does not tip the other way to result in an irrevocable, often fatal, hyperinflammatory state. In a recent case study, single cell RNA sequencing analysis performed on the peripheral blood mononuclear cells of a relapsed ENKTL patient before and after treatment with anti-PD1 therapy (penpulimab) revealed marked reduction in myeloid cells and significant increase in T and NK cells with enhanced cytotoxicity following anti-PD1 treatment. The patient deteriorated and succumbed to a hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like syndrome one month after anti-PD1 therapy, which was likely related to overactivated cytotoxic T/NK lymphocyte response causing systemic hyperinflammation and excessive killing capacity following anti-PD1 therapy.
115
This case raises concerns regarding the safety and efficacy of PD1 inhibitor therapy in patients with EBV-associated lymphomas.

Molecular and microenvironmental factors associated with prognosis
Recent molecular classifications of ENKTL by Xiong et al., Dong et al., Chen et al., and Ito et al. have identified several genetic features with significant prognostic implications (

Epigenetic modifications, particularly mutations in histone modifiers, show variable prognostic effects. Predictive biomarkers for treatment response
Predictive biomarkers indicate how well a patient will respond to a specific treatment. In recent years, there have also been a number of predictive biomarkers proposed for ENKTL. With asparaginase-based chemotherapy combinations becoming standard of care for frontline treatment of ENKTL, there have been attempts to identify patients who may have suboptimal response to it. One such study found that patients with methylated
PTPRK
promoter regions treated with the pegasparaginase-based SMILE protocol have an inferior overall survival.
137
Similarly, high expression of the
ASNS
gene was associated with worse response to asparaginase-based therapy due to asparaginase resistance.
16
In a retrospective analysis of patients with relapsed/refractory ENKTL, cryptic rearrangements in the 3′-UTR of the PD-L1 gene were found to be predictive of response to pembrolizumab treatment.
111
Non-coding RNAs, such as miRNAs have also been linked to ENKTL biological activity and treatment efficacy. Higher plasma levels of miRNA-155 were observed in patients with stable disease or progression after 2 cycles of chemotherapy compared to those with partial and complete remission.

In addition to the above, activating mutations in JAK/STAT have also been shown to predict response to the JAK1 inhibitor, ruxolitinib, in a Phase II clinical trial

although JAK inhibitors are still not routinely used in the treatment of this disease outside the context of a clinical trial.
Conclusion
Advances in next generation sequencing have significantly enhanced our understanding of the molecular pathogenesis of ENKTL, leading to the discovery of novel molecular classification and prognostic models. Recent studies have also shed light on the pivotal role of the TME in disease biology, identifying key cellular and molecular subsets with potential therapeutic and prognostic implications. However, despite these promising developments, they remain in the early stages of clinical application.
At present, clinical management of ENKTL still relies on conventional Lugano staging by FDG-PET and traditional prognostication models such as PINK and PINK-E (age >60 years old, Stage III/IV disease, non-nasal localisation, distant lymph node involvement ± detectable plasma EBV levels).
8
Owing to their high levels of expression of P-glycoprotein and consequently, multidrug resistance (MDR) phenotype, ENKTL responds poorly to anthracycline-based chemotherapy regimens designed for conventional high grade B-cell lymphomas.
140
The standard-of-care for Stage I/II ENKTL remains asparaginase-containing regimens combined with radiotherapy. At present, there are no prospective randomized studies to guide how these two treatment modalities ought to be sequenced, and centres typically adopt regimens based on local institutional protocols and access to timely radiotherapy. In Stage III/IV disease, current standard-of-care is the use of asparaginase-based combination chemotherapy. Of these, the SMILE (steroid [dexamethasone], methotrexate, ifosfamide,
l
-asparaginase, and etoposide) regimen
141
is one of the most widely used, although alternative regimens, such as AspaMetDex (
l
-asparaginase, methotrexate, and dexamethasone)
142
and P-GEMOX combining gemcitabine, oxaliplatin and pegaspargase regimen
143
are also in use. As with Stage I/II disease, the treatment of choice for Stage III/IV ENKTL is often guided by institutional expertise and access to the drugs.
140
With a deeper understanding of the processes driving ENKTL biology—including genetic, epigenetic, and TME interactions—there is hope that future approaches will shift towards precision medicine and individualized treatment modalities. With the continued development of single-cell spatial technologies (sc-Spatial-omics), the role of the TME will become even more critical in shaping our understanding of tumor behavior and therapeutic insensitivity. In particular, sc-Spatial-omics can potentially uncover tumor heterogeneity and identify clonal evolution within tumors for personalized therapy selection and to predict resistance mechanisms. Identification of macrophage and tumor/immune–cell interactions and exhausted T-cell phenotypes can guide ICI therapy, and monitoring the crosstalks between tumor, immune and stromal cells in response to therapy may possibly identify resistant clones before clinical relapse However, many current spatial transcriptomic technologies have yet to offer single-cell resolution and complex computational methods to integrate data are required.
